findings.title: Conflicts with Al Noor GCC non-compete (in force until 14 Sep 2029): Saudi Arabia
findings.explanation: Signed Al Noor MSA cl. 12.1 bars AtliQ and its Affiliates from analytics/AI/revenue-management work for any 'Hospitality Business' in the GCC, wherever the work is performed. Cl. 1.11 defines that as anyone who owns or operates hotels, resorts or serviced apartments, or who provides distribution, revenue-management or guest-analytics services to them (so hotel booking platforms count too). This draft covers that kind of work touching Saudi Arabia. The Feb 2026 waiver covered the Seaside Hotels (Muscat) SOW only and does not help here. Evidence in this draft: 1.1 **Gulf Crown Hotels & Resorts Co.**, a closed joint stock company incorporated under the laws of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, holding Commercial Registration No. 1010584431, with its head office at King Fahd Road, Al Olaya District, P.O. Box 88214, Riyadh 11662, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (the "**Company**"); and / 2.1 WHEREAS the Company owns and operates a portfolio of hotels and resorts within the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and wishes to modernise its commercial and guest-facing operations in line with its Digital Transformation Programme; / 3.6 "**Business Day**" means any day other than a Friday, Saturday or official public holiday in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
findings.suggestion: Do not sign until one of: (a) a new written waiver from Al Noor under cl. 12.4 (as done for Seaside, Feb 2026); (b) GCC properties carved out of scope; or (c) counsel (Mehta Rao) confirms the restriction does not apply. Do not tell the client anything firm yet (counsel's advice, 25 Sep).
findings.quote: the Supplier undertakes that neither it nor any of its Affiliates shall, during the Restricted Period, directly or indirectly, provide data analytics, artificial intelligence or revenue-management services to any Hospitality Business in the GCC.
findings.precedent: 22 Sep queue meeting: nobody could find the Al Noor contract; Bhavin thought it had expired. It runs to 14 Sep 2029.

findings.title: Liquidated damages: calculated on the total contract value, not the delayed milestone, no exclusion for delay the client causes
findings.explanation: AtliQ would owe delay damages with calculated on the total contract value, not the delayed milestone, no exclusion for delay the client causes. Checklist: 'LDs → cap it. never open ended'.
findings.suggestion: Counter with AtliQ's standard: 0.5% of the affected milestone fee per complete week of delay attributable to the supplier, capped at 5% of that milestone fee, no LDs for client-caused or force-majeure delay, LDs as sole remedy for delay.
findings.quote: 12.2 Should the Service Provider fail to achieve any Milestone by its scheduled completion date, the Service Provider shall pay to the Company, by way of liquidated damages and not as a penalty, an amount equal to one percent (1%) of the Contract Value for each week or part thereof of delay.
findings.precedent: Brightwater: uncapped 1%/day LD + no client-delay carve-out → $9k settlement + $14.2k legal fees. Acme, Northwind, Trustline all accepted 0.5%/week of milestone, cap 5%. Al Noor's 10% total cap was a one-off strategic exception.

findings.title: Foreign governing law: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
findings.explanation: Governing law is Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Karandeep's checklist: 'gov law → ours (India for Pvt Ltd, US for Inc)'. AtliQ has no presence there and would have to litigate abroad.
findings.suggestion: Ask for Indian law with Mumbai/Pune arbitration (Pvt Ltd) or a US state (Inc); fall back to a neutral seat such as SIAC/LCIA arbitration.
findings.quote: governed by the laws of Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
findings.precedent: Al Noor: DIFC law was accepted as the client's 'group standard'. Onshore Saudi/UAE law is a different, less predictable forum.

findings.title: Payment term 60 days
findings.explanation: Payment in 60 days; checklist says '30 days, 45 max'.
findings.quote: 5.3 The Company shall pay each undisputed invoice within sixty (60) days from the date of receipt of a valid invoice.

context_notes.name: 2026-09-22_internal_contract_queue.md
context_notes.body:
# Internal — contract queue (ad-hoc, 22 Sep)
Present: Karandeep, Bhavin, Dhaval, Jay

Called because three people chased Karandeep on the same morning.

Queue as of today (from Jay's list on the whiteboard):
- Harrington (Dhaval) — $210k, US, their paper — by **1 Oct**
- Lakeshore (Jay) — $64k, US — by **3 Oct**
- BlueOrchid pilot (Jay) — $38k — by **5 Oct**
- Gulf Crown (Bhavin) — $140k, Saudi — by **10 Oct**
- TravelHub (Karandeep) — $52k, Dubai — no date
- Rheinwerk (Bhavin) — €88k, Munich — draft arriving tomorrow, by **15 Oct**
- Sunrise SOW-2 (Dhaval) — $45k — Meera sending this week, wants by **8 Oct**

Discussion:
- Karandeep: reviewing late at night after calls, 10pm onwards. A client-paper MSA takes him 3–4 hrs properly. "Harrington alone is a whole evening and I haven't started."
- Dhaval raised ShopSwift — SOW sat 9 days in July waiting for review, Elena's budget slipped a quarter. "We lost that one to our own queue."
- Volume: Bhavin reckons last year was ~5 contracts/month, this year ~9 (MSAs, SOWs, NDAs, DPAs, amendments). Only Karandeep signs.
- Went through Gulf Crown headline terms. Midway Karandeep stopped: "didn't we sign something with the Dubai hotel people that stops us doing hotels in the Gulf?"
- Nobody could find the Al Noor contract quickly — Dhaval searched the shared drive, not there. Karandeep thinks it's in his email "somewhere".
- Bhavin: "I think that expired, no? It was a 2025 thing." Karandeep not sure.
- Jay: "is there a list of what we've agreed to not do?" — silence.
- Dhaval asked if we should send Harrington to counsel. Karandeep: "it's $210k, but Mehta Rao takes a week." Not decided.
- Bhavin: Gulf Crown can't slip, Faisal has a summit on the 14th.

Karandeep will go through them this weekend.

*(No owner, order of review, or deadline per contract was agreed. The Al Noor contract was not located during the meeting.)*

llm_summary: The headline risk is not in this contract's wording: signing it puts AtliQ in breach of the Al Noor GCC non-compete, and clause 9.1(d) would make that a false warranty from day one. Beyond that, data-protection liability is uncapped and guest data must stay in Saudi Arabia, which clashes with a Pune delivery team.
llm_questions: Has Al Noor been asked for a waiver for Saudi Arabia, or is this deal off the table until Sep 2029?
Will any Gulf Crown guest data be viewed from Pune, and does Gulf Crown know that?
Who will review the Arabic version before signing?

findings.title: AtliQ warrants it has no conflicting restrictions
findings.quote: it is not bound by any agreement or restriction which would prevent or restrict it from performing the Services for the Company.
findings.explanation: AtliQ promises it is free of any restriction that would stop it doing this work.
findings.suggestion: Check existing commitments before giving this warranty, or qualify it with a disclosure schedule.
findings.judge_reasoning: With the Al Noor non-compete in force until Sep 2029, AtliQ would be in breach of this warranty the moment it signs. This turns a commitment conflict into a direct claim by Gulf Crown as well.

findings.title: Guest data must stay in Saudi Arabia
findings.quote: Guest Data shall be hosted within the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia unless the Company provides prior written approval for any transfer outside the Kingdom.
findings.explanation: Engineers in Pune viewing production data could count as a transfer outside the Kingdom.
findings.suggestion: Get written approval for remote access from India, or commit to a KSA-hosted environment with masked data offshore.
findings.judge_reasoning: A real delivery constraint, but it is solvable with written approval or a KSA-hosted workspace, so it is a negotiation point rather than a blocker.

findings.title: Deliverables only transfer on payment in full
findings.quote: All Deliverables specifically created for the Company under this Agreement shall, upon payment in full, become the property of the Company.
findings.explanation: Ownership passes to the client only after full payment.
findings.judge_reasoning: This protects AtliQ: the client does not own anything until it has paid. Keep it.

findings.title: Confidentiality survives five years
findings.quote: The obligations in this Clause 7 shall survive for a period of five (5) years following the expiry or termination of this Agreement.
findings.explanation: Confidentiality lasts five years after the contract ends.
findings.judge_reasoning: Five years is market standard and mutual.

findings.title: Uncapped liability for data protection and confidentiality breaches
findings.quote: Save in respect of liability arising from fraud, wilful misconduct, breach of Clause 7 (Confidentiality) or Clause 13 (Data Protection), each Party's aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the Contract Value.
findings.explanation: A guest-data incident across nine hotels sits outside the USD 140,000 cap, so exposure is unlimited.
findings.suggestion: Add a super-cap for data protection breaches, e.g. 2x the Contract Value.
findings.judge_reasoning: Correct. Guest data for 2,500+ rooms sits outside the cap; the playbook says never accept unlimited liability.
findings.precedent: PayTrack (Jan 2025): Karandeep held the liability cap at 1x fees.

findings.title: Arabic text prevails over English
findings.quote: In the event of any inconsistency, the Arabic text shall prevail.
findings.explanation: Nobody at AtliQ reads Arabic, so the binding version is one AtliQ has not reviewed.
findings.suggestion: Ask for English to prevail, or get the Arabic version checked by counsel before signing.
findings.judge_reasoning: Standard in KSA government-linked paper, but AtliQ should not sign a binding text it cannot read.

findings.title: Termination for convenience pays only for accepted work
findings.quote: the Company shall pay for all Services performed and accepted up to the date of termination.
findings.explanation: Work in progress on a milestone that is not yet accepted would go unpaid.
findings.suggestion: Pay for work performed up to termination, accepted or not, plus reasonable demobilisation costs.
findings.judge_reasoning: With milestones up to 10 weeks long, up to USD 42,000 of work could go unpaid on a convenience exit.
